title: Block close: the last page
hook: the Bible begins in a garden and ends in a garden-city

segments.voice: Yesterday, watchful: lamps lit, and a master who comes home and serves. Your line was ready, not afraid. What good were you found doing? Day one thousand three hundred thirty-one.

Bookends hold a row of books upright, one at each end. Read the Bible that way, and look at its two ends. At the front: a garden, a river, a tree of life, and two people sent out of it, with the way back closed behind them. At the back: a river again, and the tree of life again, but this time the river and the tree stand in the middle of a city, and the gates are open. A river, a tree, a different place. Everything else sits between them. Today we close this block of the path by reading both ends at once.
screen: `A GARDEN AT THE FRONT, A CITY AT THE BACK.`
`A RIVER, A TREE, A DIFFERENT PLACE.`

segments.voice: First, the garden. Genesis says God planted it, with "the tree of life also in the midst of the garden," and "a river went out of Eden to water the garden." The man is put there "to dress it and to keep it." Then the break. The man and woman are sent out, and the way to the tree of life is guarded, as this block saw beside the healing leaves. Second, the city. Revelation's last chapter shows "a pure river of water of life, clear as crystal," and in the street of the city, on either side of the river, "was there the tree of life." And: "Blessed are they that do his commandments, that they may have right to the tree of life, and may enter in through the gates into the city." The guarded way is open. Third, why a city and not just the garden again? Some readers notice that the story doesn't rewind. A city is where people live together: streets, gates, neighbors, work. And work is there at both ends. The garden had to be dressed and kept; in the city, "his servants shall serve him." The ending keeps the garden at its heart and wraps human life around it. Fourth, look back at this block. We opened Revelation as an apocalypse, an unveiling. We met the Alpha and Omega on Patmos, read the letters to the churches, stood in the throne room before a slain Lamb, watched riders, heard silence in heaven, and saw Babylon fall and a wedding feast laid. Then a new heaven and a new earth, and Christian hope up close: memento mori, the art of dying, funerals, praying for the dead, a seed in the ground, a taunt to death, heaven coming down, face to face, grief with hope, and a lamp kept burning.
screen: `FROM UNVEILING TO A LAMP KEPT BURNING.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: picture the garden-city. Settle, and breathe. Let a city come to mind, the one you live in or one you love: its streets, its noise, its people going to work. Now set a river down the middle of the main street, clear as crystal, and a tree on either bank. Keep the shops and the buses. Keep the neighbors. Just let the river and the tree be at the center. If you pray, you can hold that picture before God. If you don't, simply stay inside it for a minute. The bell holds the time.
Block close. The end of this block on Revelation and Christian hope: the Bible's last page, where the garden comes back, inside a city.

Your line: from garden to city. Today, notice one green thing growing in the middle of something built: a tree in a parking lot, weeds in a sidewalk crack, a plant on an office desk. Tomorrow a new block opens: rites, spaces and the arts of church life. Day one thousand three hundred thirty-one.

howItsDone: Some Christians read Genesis 1–3 and Revelation 21–22 together as the Bible's bookends, and some churches read the closing chapters of Revelation in the season after Easter.
